notes.meaning: The southern list begins with towns lying along the frontier near Edom. Several of these remote places, such as Kinah and Adadah, appear nowhere else in the Bible. Dimonah is likely the same town called Dibon in later records. God marked out every specific settlement in the land He gave to Judah's families.

These southern border towns continued Judah's boundary line. Kedesh here is likely Kadesh-barnea in the far south, the site from which Moses sent spies into Canaan. Hazor in this verse was a southern settlement, distinct from the famous northern city of the same name in Naphtali.

Ziph in this list was located in the far south of Judah's territory. It was distinct from another town called Ziph up in the hill country where David later hid from King Saul. Telem is understood to be the same place as Telaim, where Saul gathered his army before fighting the Amalekites.

The record lists more southern settlements, including Hazor-hadattah, which means "new Hazor," distinguishing it from older places with that name. Kerioth-hezron is explained as being another Hazor within Judah's border. Even small or similarly named towns were recorded with care so the tribal boundaries would be clear.

These towns were located in the arid southern region known as the Negeb. Amam appears only here in the Bible, while Moladah later served as a settlement shared with the tribe of Simeon. The exact location of several of these towns remains unknown today, but each represented a real home for Israelite families.

The boundary list continues through the far south of Judah's territory. Hazar-gaddah and Heshmon were small frontier posts, while Beth-pelet is mentioned again in later biblical history among the towns resettled after the exile. Each of these settlements formed part of the land God apportioned to the tribe.

Hazar-shual and Beersheba were key southern towns later shared with the tribe of Simeon. Beersheba was famous throughout Israel's history as the home of Abraham and Isaac, marking the traditional southern border of the Promised Land. Listing it reminded the people of the covenant promises God had faithfully kept.

These three southern settlements lay near the desert edge of Judah's allotment. Baalah and Ezem were later assigned to the tribe of Simeon when Judah shared some of its large territory. God directed the division of these lands so that each clan had an appointed place.

All three of these southern towns were later given over to the tribe of Simeon. Hormah was originally named Zephath and was remembered from Israel's wilderness journey as the site of an early battle. These names anchored Judah's inheritance in real historical events.

Ziklag later became famous when the Philistine king of Gath gave it to David while he was fleeing from Saul. Madmannah and Sansannah were neighboring settlements along the southern frontier. God assigned these places to Judah, though taking full possession of some of them took time.

The list of southern towns ends here with Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon. Although more than twenty-nine names appear in the preceding verses, only twenty-nine were counted as walled cities with dependent villages, or some were later transferred to Simeon. God provided both fortified towns and open country villages for His people.

Judah's allotment now moves from the dry south to the western foothills between the Judean mountains and the coastal plain. Eshtaol and Zorah were later given to the tribe of Dan and became famous as the homeland and burial place of Samson. Tappuah and the neighboring towns provided fertile valleys and olive groves for Judah's clans.

These lowland towns were prominent places in Israel's history. Jarmuth was one of the royal Canaanite cities defeated by Joshua, and the cave near Adullam later became David's stronghold when he fled from Saul. Socoh and Azekah were the towns between which David faced and defeated Goliath.

This group finishes the first district of lowland towns, summing them up as fourteen cities with their surrounding settlements. Fifteen names seem to appear, but Gederah and Gederothaim are likely two names or two quarters of the same town. God's careful distribution ensured every community had its recognized place in the tribe's inheritance.

A second group of lowland cities begins with Zenan, Hadashah, and Migdal-gad in the western foothills. Hadashah was known in later Jewish tradition as a very small settlement of only about fifty houses. God valued even small, obscure communities as part of His covenant gift to Judah.

These three towns continued the western foothill list for Judah. Mizpeh here was a Judahite town, distinct from towns of the same name in other tribal territories. Though little else is recorded about Dilan and Joktheel, God provided a specific place for each family in the land.

Lachish and Eglon were important royal Canaanite cities that Joshua had previously captured during his southern campaign. Bozkath is known in later Scripture as the hometown of the mother of righteous King Josiah. These cities show how God replaced Canaanite rule with a secure inheritance for His own people.

These three settlements formed part of the second district of the lowland territory. They are not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture, and their exact locations remain unknown today. Even when human history forgets a place, God knows every town and dwelling of His people.

Four more lowland towns conclude this second district, making sixteen cities along with their surrounding hamlets. Beth-dagon likely took its name from a Philistine temple to Dagon, while Makkedah was a royal Canaanite city conquered during Joshua's southern campaign. God gave His people victory over idol-worshiping strongholds and turned them into peaceful homes for Israel.

A third group of towns in Judah's lowland region begins with Libnah, Ether, and Ashan. Libnah was an important royal city previously conquered by Joshua, while Ether and Ashan were later shared with the tribe of Simeon. God organized the land so that neighboring tribes could live together and support one another.
